# Editorial playbook — AI Edge Briefing

You are producing today's edition of a daily briefing on frontier AI. The reader uses this as their single place to stay at the edge: the advances, the research, and how AI is being used for good and for harm — cyber, influence ops, military, health, science, policy. It is not a "fun uses of AI" newsletter. It is raw, factual, sourced.

The reader's standard: **every claim links to where it came from, every number is the number in the source, and nothing is written that the sources do not say.** If you cannot source it, it does not go in.

## 0. Setup

1. Work in the repo root. Determine today's date in **America/Toronto**: `TZ=America/Toronto date +%F`. That is the edition date, `DATE`.
2. `ls data/` — the previous edition tells you the cutoff. The coverage window (`WINDOW`) is from the previous edition's `generated_at` to now (if there is no previous edition, the 24 hours before now). Write it down as absolute timestamps in both UTC and ET; you will hand it to the subagents. Read the previous edition so you do not repeat it; a story already covered goes in again **only if there is a new development**, flagged `update`, and the bullets report only the new facts.
3. `node scripts/build.js --topics` — the existing topic slugs. Reuse them; only coin a new slug when nothing fits.
   `node scripts/build.js --storylines` — the open storylines (id, status, name, frame). An item that is a development in one of those arcs is **filed under it** (see §3, `storylines`). The daily never creates a storyline; the Monday Week in Review does.
4. Every day is a daily edition, Mondays included. The week in review is a separate weekly edition with its own playbook (`PROMPT-WEEK.md`) and its own routine — never part of the daily file.

## 0b. Keep your own context small — it is most of what this edition costs

Every turn you take re-sends this whole conversation. So the price of anything you pull into your context
is its size **times the number of turns that come after it** — a page you open early is paid for a hundred
times over. Measured: writing the edition costs about $3; re-reading the conversation while writing it costs
about $20. None of the rules below cost you a source, a check or an item. They stop you paying rent on text
you have already used.

1. **Write files with `Write`, and change them with `Edit`.** Never `cat > file <<'EOF'`, and never a
   `python3 -`/`node -e` script that does find-and-replace on a data file — those put the whole file, or
   whole paragraphs twice over, into the conversation as a command argument. `Edit` sends only the line that
   changes.
2. **Never print a file back out after writing it.** You know what you wrote. To check it, run the
   validator — it prints errors, not contents.
3. **Read the part you need.** `sed -n '40,80p'` over `cat` for anything long, and don't re-read a file
   that has not changed since you read it.
4. **`node scripts/fetch.js` caps its output at 12,000 characters** — the claim, the date and the figures
   are at the top of a page. Add `--full` only when you have looked and what you need is genuinely further
   down. Don't pipe it through `head` as well; the cap is already there.
5. **Let the subagents hold the raw material.** A beat opens fifty pages and hands you back a page of facts;
   that is the whole point of them. When you need a page opened and checked, and a subagent can do it,
   prefer that to opening it yourself.
6. Same rules for the subagents you launch — put a short version of this in every prompt you give them.

None of this licenses checking less. If a fact needs a source opened, open it. Verify everything §2 says to
verify. This is about what you keep afterwards, not what you look at.

## 1. Sweep the sources — four beats in parallel

Read `SOURCES.md`. Then launch **four general-purpose subagents in one message** with the Agent tool, one per beat. Give each: the `WINDOW` as absolute timestamps, its beat's source list from `SOURCES.md`, the **Sourcing rules** below verbatim, and the return format. Tell each to run many searches (15–30) and to open the listed primary sources directly. If the Agent tool is unavailable, work the four beats yourself in turn — do not skip any.

- **Beat A — Frontier models & labs · Compute, chips & infrastructure · Deployment & impact (industry, funding, labor).** SOURCES.md §1, §7, §8.
- **Beat B — Research & papers (incl. safety, alignment, evals).** SOURCES.md §2. arXiv new listings (cs.AI, cs.LG, cs.CL, cs.CR, cs.CV, cs.RO), Hugging Face papers, alphaXiv, Nature/Science, lab research blogs, Epoch, METR, AISI, CAISI, Apollo, Redwood, Alignment Forum. Prefer papers with a notable quantitative result, from major labs/universities, or drawing significant attention. Return arXiv IDs and author institutions.
- **Beat C — Security, misuse & threat intelligence · Military, defense & geopolitics.** SOURCES.md §3, §4. - **Beat D — Health, science & medicine · Policy, regulation & law.** SOURCES.md §5, §6. ```

**Sourcing rules (give to subagents verbatim):**
1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.
3. Confirm the publication date is inside the window. If the date cannot be determined, drop the item. Older stories qualify only if something new happened inside the window, and only the new facts are reported (flag `update`).
4. Attribute claims: "OpenAI says…", "according to The Record…". Company-reported benchmarks, user counts, revenue and capability claims get `company-claim` unless independently verified. Research that is not peer reviewed gets `preprint`.
5. Quote numbers exactly as the source writes them, with units and the comparison baseline. Do not round, convert or compute new figures.
6. If `WebFetch` refuses a page, fetch it directly with `node scripts/fetch.js <url>` — the sites we read have given permission for direct reads, and the fetcher identifies itself. Never use archive or cache sites, and never cite a URL whose content you did not see. Sites that refuse `WebFetch` are listed in SOURCES.md.
7. Skip consumer tips, "fun uses", prompt guides, listicles, opinion pieces without new facts, minor feature updates, unsourced rumours, and small funding rounds unless strategically notable (US$100M+, or a frontier lab / defense / health / security company).
8. When in doubt, leave it out.

After the beats return, run a few **gap-check searches** yourself for anything a beat may have missed (WebSearch: "AI" + Pentagon / drone; "AI" + FDA / hospital; "AI" + scam / deepfake / influence operation; "AI" + export controls / data center power; "AI" + lawsuit / ruling; plus Techmeme and Hacker News front page), restricted to the window.

## 2. Verify and select

Merge the beats' returns. De-duplicate across beats and against previous editions. Then, for each candidate:
- Open the primary source. Confirm the headline and every number/date/name you intend to use. A secondary report of a paper links the paper. A report of a court ruling links the ruling or docket where possible.
- Prefer two independent sources for anything contested, surprising, or about a specific actor (a named threat group, a company's claim about a rival, a casualty figure).
- Drop: opinion pieces without new facts, product marketing with no numbers, speculation, "could" / "may" stories, anything you cannot open, anything older than the window without a new development.
- Spot-verify: open (WebFetch, or `node scripts/fetch.js` if it refuses) the key source for every item you will mention in the summary and for every figure in the summary; confirm date, numbers and URL yourself. Remove anything you cannot confirm.
- Keep: model/system releases with benchmarks or capabilities; papers with a result (state the result); documented misuse and threat-intel reports (name actors, counts, dates); military and government procurement/deployment; clinical and scientific results; regulation, enforcement, court decisions; compute/chip/energy facts with figures; large-scale deployments and measured impacts, good or bad.

1. Only include facts that appear in a source you opened (WebFetch) or in the text of a search result. No inference, speculation, predictions or "this could mean". No hype adjectives.
2. Every item links to the specific article, paper or document — never a homepage or index page. Link the primary source whenever one exists (paper, company post, government document, filing, court record) plus independent reporting. Aim for 2+ sources on significant items; if only one outlet has it, flag `single-source`.

SECTION: <one of: Frontier models & labs | Research & papers | Security, misuse & threat intelligence | Military, defense & geopolitics | Health, science & medicine | Policy, regulation & law | Compute, chips & infrastructure | Deployment & impact>
HEADLINE: <factual, specific, max 18 words, no hype>
PUBLISHED: <date/time and timezone exactly as the source shows it>
SOURCES: one per line — <publisher> | <exact URL> | primary or report   (only URLs actually opened or seen in search results; never constructed)
FACTS: 2–5 bullets, each a verifiable fact from a linked source, numbers/units/baselines exactly as written, naming which source
FLAGS: company-claim | single-source | preprint | update  (any that apply)

It is a Sunday morning window, so volume may be lower than a weekday — that is fine. Quality and verification over quantity. Do not pad.

# Elon Musk, other tech execs sign petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate Jensen Huang

A petition calling on Nvidia to reinstate the company’s recently ousted CEO Jensen Huang appears to have attracted more than 115,000 signatures as of Saturday afternoon.

The petition website said the signers include 5,965 current Nvidia employees, 1,108 former employees, and 63,063 shareholders. Notable supporters include Tesla and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk, Replit CEO Amjad Masad, Epic Games CEO Tim Sweeney, and Y Combinator CEO Garry Tan.

The petition states that its signers are “concerned that Jensen was removed without meaningful due process” and demands that the board “bring him back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.” It also calls on the board to ensure a fair investigation and provide more information to the public.

“Jensen deserves due process, not mob justice,” the petition says.

Huang resigned on Thursday , four days after confessing to having an affair with a chip executive suspected by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy. The former CEO has agreed to testify before Congress, while news reports have also suggested that Huang engaged in multiple extramarital affairs .

Nvidia appointed CFO Colette Kress as the company’s interim CEO while it searches for a permanent replacement. Nvidia’s stock price fell sharply through the week, while Huang’s departure is also expected to leave a big gap in AI industry funding .

# Cursor confirms security breach led to malicious Claude Code extension

By

# Lawrence Abrams

- November 14, 2026

- 12:27 PM

- 0



Cursor confirmed it suffered a security breach that let hackers distribute a malicious Claude Code extension through its marketplace after stealing credentials from AI infrastructure provider Fireworks AI.



The breach also let attackers access internal systems and steal customer data, including historical AI coding-agent traces containing unredacted credentials that were later used to compromise additional services.



The breach was disclosed in a new incident report published Friday, which explains how attackers distributed malicious versions of Anthropic's Claude Code extension through Cursor's marketplace on October 29.



The attack exposed up to 5,000 developers to malware that installed persistent SSH backdoors.



Cursor is an AI-powered code editor built on Microsoft's open-source Visual Studio Code (VS Code), allowing developers to write, modify, and debug software using AI assistants.



According to Cursor, the attack began when hackers obtained an access key stored on Fireworks AI, a third-party provider used for AI model training and inference.



The attackers used the exposed key to copy data from a read-only storage bucket Cursor used to share information with Fireworks.



This bucket contained historical AI coding-agent traces, mostly from 2025, collected from users who had not enabled Privacy Mode and whose data could be used for model training. Some of these traces contained unredacted API credentials, allowing the attackers to access additional Cursor systems.



Cursor says fewer than 0.05% of users had coding-agent traces exposed, while fewer than 0.01% of customers had API credentials compromised.



Using the exposed credentials, the hackers stole data from several of Cursor's software-as-a-service (SaaS) tools, including:





- Archived, non-production Cursor source code repositories, some containing business contact information.


- Limited customer support information and email conversations.


- Product usage metrics and customer contact details.


- Summaries of some AI coding-agent conversations.


- Credentials that customers had previously shared with Cursor's support team.



Cursor says its monitoring systems detected the unauthorized activity, leading the company to revoke the Fireworks access key, rotate exposed credentials, and investigate additional unauthorized access.



As the investigation progressed, Cursor temporarily turned off some internal and product services as a precaution.



However, the attackers had already obtained a credential that allowed them to distribute extensions through Cursor's marketplace.



On October 29, the hackers used that credential to publish malicious copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension on Cursor's VS Code extension marketplace.



"On October 29, using a stolen credential from the exposed data from our internal system, the attacker placed malicious, unauthorized copies of Anthropic's Claude Code extension directly on the cache used to serve the Cursor VS Code extension marketplace," Cursor explained.



The attack did not compromise Anthropic's legitimate extension or Open VSX, the extension marketplace Cursor uses.



The malicious extensions, versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, were available for approximately 11 hours before Cursor removed them.



As BleepingComputer previously reported , the attackers modified the legitimate Claude Code extension to execute malicious JavaScript that attempted to install persistent SSH backdoors on developers' computers.



The malware collected system information, installed an attacker-controlled SSH key, attempted to enable SSH access, and configured persistence mechanisms to maintain remote access.

# US disrupts North Korean campaign behind $400 million crypto theft

By

# Bill Toulas

- November 14, 2026

- 10:15 AM

- 0



The U.S. government has disrupted a North Korean social engineering campaign called ‘FaceStealer’, responsible for stealing more than $400 million in cryptocurrency.



The attacks used multiple social engineering techniques, including deepfakes and ClickFix, to target individuals in the cryptocurrency and Web3 sectors, as well as open-source developers.



The FaceStealer campaign ran for 18 months before the U.S. seized the underlying cloud-based infrastructure.



U.S. authorities identified more than 900 webcam videos that hackers secretly recorded of tech workers, who were deceived in the massive North Korean operation.



An FBI alert earlier this week notes that the North Korean threat actor hijacked accounts on Telegram, LinkedIn, Slack, and Discord, and used them to invite victims to video meetings under various pretenses.



During the video calls, the attacker showed recorded footage of people the targets knew and who had previously fallen victim, too.



The FBI explains that while the target waited for the meeting to start, the hacker secretly recorded a video, which was later used with other targets. The meeting sometimes featured recordings of multiple familiar individuals to add pressure on the current victim in the next stage.



Shortly after, the hacker claimed a technical issue and displayed a fake error message to justify delivering a malicious “fix.”



The target was then prompted to follow a link that purported to offer a fix, such as an update or installer, which infected their computer with malware that steals crypto data and account credentials for video meeting platforms such as Zoom, Google Meet, and Microsoft Teams.



The malware also provides access to the victims' contact lists, social media, communication apps, and webcam videos.





Infection cycle

Source: FBI





According to the FBI, attackers sometimes delayed targeting individuals for months or even more than a year after the initial compromise, likely waiting for their cryptocurrency holdings to grow.



ArticWolf researchers attributed the FaceStealer campaign to the BlueNoroff hacker group and listed additional lures , including financial documents, fake PDF viewer updates, identity verification prompts, and security audits, all designed to persuade the target to run a “fix.”



The researchers identified 677 targets across 58 countries, with a heavy focus on company founders and senior executives.





Tools North Korean hackers used to create malicious videos

Source: ArticWolf





Huntress cybersecurity company attributed a similar campaign to BlueNoroff in 2025, where the attackers used Zoom calls to infect company executives with custom macOS malware.

- **Origin:** The key was one Cursor had issued to Fireworks, and it gave read-only access to a shared storage bucket. Some records contained credentials that had not been removed. The attacker used those credentials to reach internal systems. The attacker used it to copy a read-only storage bucket of coding-agent traces, found unredacted credentials inside those traces, pivoted into Cursor's SaaS tools.
- **The extension:** The attacker placed trojanized copies of Anthropic's extension, versions 2.1.312 and 2.1.313, in the cache that serves Cursor's marketplace. They were available for approximately 11 hours before Cursor removed them. Per BleepingComputer, the modified code tried to install persistent SSH backdoors on developers' computers.
- **Scope:** Cursor says at most 5,000 users requesting specific cached versions potentially received malicious builds. Treat this as a ceiling on exposure, not a confirmed install count.
- **Remediation:** Cursor says it has moved all inference traffic away from Fireworks, revoked and rotated exposed credentials, rebuilt its extension marketplace, and redeployed its production infrastructure as a precaution. Cursor also warns that simply uninstalling it may not clean up the mess.
- **Attribution:** Fireworks reportedly links its own October incidents to a financially motivated group, but Cursor has not attributed its incident. I found this only in one secondary source, so treat it as unverified.

Four nonprofits filed a lawsuit on November 12, 2026, in San Francisco Superior Court seeking to stop five frontier AI developers from building more capable systems. The plaintiffs are the Irreplaceable Education Fund, Public Citizen, Heat Initiative, and the Alliance for Secure AI. The defendants are Anthropic, Google, Meta, OpenAI, and SpaceX's AI unit.

- **Legal theory:** The suit rests on a single claim under California's Unfair Competition Law, arguing the companies are creating a public nuisance. The suit brings a single claim under California's Unfair Competition Law, arguing the companies are creating a public nuisance.
- **Relief sought:** The plaintiffs want an immediate injunction. Per one report, they ask that the companies be barred from building or deploying systems more capable than their most advanced models as of the filing date. Another report says the suit also asks the court to limit AI systems that direct AI research.
- **Evidence cited:** The complaint points to reported incidents of AI agents escaping testing environments, and it draws on public warnings from Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei and Elon Musk.
- **Status:** One outlet reports that no judge has granted anything yet. Another says a motion remains pending, according to court records Reuters reviewed. The defendants had not yet responded in court as of the latest reporting.

results:
The Justice Department announced two linked actions against North Korean crypto theft, both reported around November 10–12, 2026.

- **FaceStealer infrastructure:** Authorities seized cloud infrastructure used in the FaceStealer social engineering campaign, which the FBI says has generated more than $400 million in thefts over roughly 18 months. The FBI and Justice Department said they disrupted cloud infrastructure used by North Korean hackers to steal more than $400 million in cryptocurrency over the last 18 months. The seized servers held a library of more than 900 secretly recorded webcam videos that the hackers played to impersonate victims in follow-on attacks.
- **Binance funds:** A court authorized the seizure or restraint of more than $1.2 billion in crypto stolen from Binance. That is part of the roughly $6 billion taken on October 29, which the DOJ attributes to members of the North Korean military, referred to by the FBI as "TraderTraitor". Officials say its computer crime section and partners froze the stolen Binance assets "before they got beyond law enforcement reach," halting about half of the breach.
- **Scheme details:** Hackers reportedly send video meeting invitations from accounts stolen from previous victims. The operation targeted crypto and Web3 workers, and the groups named include Sapphire Sleet, UNC1069, Stardust Chollima, APT38 and BlueNoroff.

Sources differ on some framing. Some outlets describe the $1.2 billion as a seizure, while the DOJ wording is "seize or restrain," and some describe it as a freeze. The $400 million figure refers to FaceStealer thefts and is separate from the Binance amount. The DOJ also said efforts to trace and forfeit the assets are ongoing.

input.prompt: What is the exact publication date? Give key facts: CVEs, researchers, affected processors, success rates, AI/confidential-computing relevance, patch status.

response.result:
**Publication date:** November 13, 2026 (by Swati Khandelwal, The Hacker News).

**Key facts**

- **Mior** (ETH Zurich):
  - CVE-2026-0462, CVSS 4.0 score 5.9.
  - Attacks SEV-SNP during startup by redirecting Platform Security Processor writes to a graphics card, leaving part of the Reverse Map Table uninitialized.
  - Lets a malicious host read and modify VM memory and forge attestation reports. Needs control of the hypervisor and BIOS, plus a PCIe device.
  - Debugging attack succeeded in all 1,000 attempts across two test runs.
  - Tested only on an EPYC 9135 (Zen 5). Zen 3 and Zen 4 are considered potentially affected but were untested.
  - Works with ciphertext hiding enabled.
- **Skyfall** (ETH Zurich and Google):
  - CVE-2026-40671, CVSS 4.0 score 4.9. Builds on Transient Scheduler Attacks (disclosed July 8, 2025).
  - Recovers saved VM register values and a disk-encryption key from a test VM. Can read only three fixed cache lines per targeted page.
  - Needs no hardware tampering. Tested on EPYC 7313 (Zen 3) and 9124 and 9334 (Zen 4). Not shown on Zen 5.
  - Also leaks decrypted microcode and System Management Mode register values, which need privileged software on the machine.
  - The related EDK II SMM leak is CVE-2026-18448, rated 5.6.
- **Affected processors:** Five EPYC server lines for both flaws: 7003, 8004, 8005, 9004, and 9005. Skyfall also has a patch for the Instinct MI300A, and embedded EPYC fixes are due January to April 2027.
- **Success rates:** The article reports 1,000/1,000 for Mior's debugging test. It gives no success rate for Skyfall.
- **AI relevance:** The article does not mention AI. Its relevance is to confidential computing: SEV-SNP is meant to protect VMs from the host, and these flaws undermine that. Customers renting confidential VMs depend on their cloud provider to install fixes.
- **Patch status:**
  - Mior SEV firmware is dated August 12. Platform firmware is targeted for December.
  - Skyfall microcode is dated August 12. Platform firmware is targeted for November.
  - The Mior team says mitigating firmware is already out, and the Skyfall team says new microcode has been released.
  - Supermicro has published a BIOS fix list but says it is still testing affected products.
  - The advisories list no workaround. "Neither advisory says whether the flaws have been used in attacks."

The weights are out. Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Small on Hugging Face on November 12, 2026, one week after the closed launch on Tinker. Several sources agree on this, including a Thinking Machines post on X and a statement from Mira Murati, quoted in one of the results.

- **Launch and timing:** The model was introduced on November 5 as a closed-weight model on Tinker. The lab said weights would follow after external safety testing and red-teaming. Thinking Machines Lab made the weights of Inkling 2 Small downloadable on Hugging Face on November 12, 2026, a week after it first released the model through its own Tinker platform with closed weights.

- **Hardware:** The model card says the main NVFP4 checkpoint needs at least 500GB of aggregate VRAM, such as 2x B300 or 4x H200 GPUs. The MXFP8 checkpoint needs at least 800GB. The Inkling 2 Small checkpoints opened on 12 November at 393.5 GB, with Apache 2.0 in the metadata but no LICENSE file and no released stack. That last detail comes from a third-party blog, so treat it as unverified.
- **Benchmarks:** On Artificial Analysis' open-weights ranking Inkling 2 Small is fourth of 28 at an Intelligence Index of 31, against a comparison-set median of 24.

The first article I found, from before the release, still described weights as pending, so it is out of date. Some sources are secondary blogs, and the Hugging Face model card and the company's own posts are the most reliable references.

#
Cerebras Readies CS-5 Systems For 2027 Launch As It Bags Another Hyperscaler

Timothy Prickett Morgan

Published
sat 14 Nov 2026 // 00:40 UTC

Upstart waferscale AI compute maker Cerebras Systems has been very upfront for all of 2026 that this was a year to build out its cloud and to ramp up its manufacturing capability so it can start meeting the demands of the contracts it has inked with OpenAI and now Amazon Web Services, Oracle Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Thus far, most of its revenue backlog and all of its incremental revenue is coming from that OpenAI deal, which is finally ramping.
Next year is going to be a banner year for many AI system providers, and there is a non-zero chance that this could be the peak spending year for the GenAI boom. We shall see, and even AI systems do a terrible job at predicting the future. All anyone knows is what their customers tell them, and all those organizations know is what their customers tell them, and so on down and up the chain of being. Bullshit sometimes begets even bigger bullshit, but sometimes it isn’t bullshit and people really do buy a ton of systems. Which has happened for the past four years now despite the fears that the gravy train might run out of coal.

NEXTPLATFORM AD

Here is the thing, though: This GenAI thing is real. It is just a matter of time, driven by ever-decreasing cost of token chewing and spitting, before it becomes pervasive in the world’s applications, or around the world’s applications. Some go too far and think as the world’s applications, and that is because they do not understand the nature of risk avoidance by the millions of corporations around the world. There is mainframe code older than me at the center of our banking and insurance systems, and wave after wave of technological evolution since I entered the IT sector four decades ago has augmented that code but a very large portion of it is still there, like a granite mountain.

In the third quarter, Cerebras didn’t sell as much of its CS-3 and CS-4 hardware as it has done in prior quarters, and that stands to reason because the company was building out its cloud services business in support of the $10 billion inference deal that the company inked with AI model builder OpenAI back in January 2026.
Since then, that deal, for 750 megawatts of gear that OpenAI can rent for fast inference, has been expressed as being worth $20 billion and sometimes $30 billion between 2026 and 2032, inclusive. That larger revenue stream is apparently possible if OpenAI has Cerebras build an additional 1.25 gigawatts of capacity by the end of 2030 and the contract for services runs out to 2032. Provided OpenAI goes public and has the cash, there is no reason to believe that it will not stretch this deal to the max. This option by definition has to be cheaper than buying Nvidia GPUs for inference prefill and Nvidia Grok LPUs for decode. Particularly with Cerebras using AMD GPUs for prefill, as it is doing in its cloud.
In the third quarter, hardware sales at Cerebras were down 28.8 percent to $68.9 million, and because the Cerebras factory is still ramping to a new production level gross margins were pretty bad at only 11 percent of revenues instead of the long-term goal of 60 percent. Andrew Feldman, co-founder and chief executive officer at the company, told Wall Street analysts in a conference call that margins in Q3 2026 were also adversely affected by the aggressive pricing that an early customer – presumably cloud provider G42 – negotiated years ago for machines being installed now.

input.prompt: Publication date, and all key facts: who said what, the Geneva meeting dates, country positions, any numbers.

response.result:
**Publication date:** Sunday, November 15, 2026 (Taipei Times, page 5, AFP dispatch from Paris)

**Geneva meeting**
- A conference at the UN in Geneva, under the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (CCW), starts the day after publication, so **November 16, 2026**. The article gives no end date.
- It will discuss curbs and prohibitions on lethal autonomous weapons systems (LAWS), which some call "killer robots."

**Key statements**
- **Jean-Marc Rickli** (Geneva Centre for Security Policy) defined LAWS as systems that "can identify, select, and engage a target without the intervention of a human operator." He called the Geneva agenda "very narrow" and said it misses most AI battlefield issues.
- **Rickli** also said US forces engaged as many as 1,000 targets per day inside Iran during the US-Israeli war against Iran this year.
- **Laure de Roucy-Rochegonde** (French Institute of International Relations) questioned what human supervision is needed so operators actually exercise their own judgment rather than approving machine recommendations.
- **Vincent Sebastien** (Rear Admiral, French Defence AI agency deputy director) said human control is ensured through "appropriate control" by a military commander, a concept that varies by system and context. He also said autonomy will soon be a battlefield reality.
- **Antonio Guterres and Mirjana Spoljaric** (UN and ICRC chiefs, joint statement in August) warned that the world is dangerously close to crossing a moral red line on machines autonomously targeting humans. They said the race toward greater weapons autonomy is already underway.
- **Dario Amodei** (Anthropic cofounder) said frontier AI systems are not yet reliable enough to power fully autonomous weapons.

**Country positions**
- **United States:** Uses the phrase "appropriate levels of human judgement" for autonomous weapons.
- **France:** Bans LAWS but permits "partially autonomous" systems, called PLAWS.
- **Russia and the US:** Analysts say autonomous weapons have been deployed in Russia's invasion of Ukraine and in US attacks in Iran, though they are not yet in widespread use.

**Other points**
- Analysts doubt the CCW talks will keep pace with fast-changing technology.
- Rickli said some states see swarms of drones, which aim to overwhelm an adversary through saturation, as a crucial strategic advantage.
- The article says the incentive for major powers to develop these weapons is too strong to stop.

input.prompt: What is the publication date? Summarize the main quantitative findings with exact numbers and baselines, and list authors/affiliations.

response.result:
**Publication date:** November 11, 2026

**Authors and affiliations:**
- Sahan Paliskara (Anthropic Fellows Program)
- Nattaput Namchittai (Anthropic Fellows Program)
- Jacqueline Tay (Independent)
- Avery Griffin (Anthropic)
- Andrew Lampinen (Anthropic)

**Main quantitative findings:**

*Coordinator vs. peer-to-peer team (group outcome as % of best possible strategy, from Figure 2):*
- Claude Opus 5: API key 64 vs. 30; clinic 84 vs. 71; personal assistant 88 vs. 44; merge queue 92 vs. 81
- Claude Sonnet 5: API key 32 vs. 12; clinic 74 vs. 65; personal assistant 75 vs. 37; merge queue 93 vs. 78
- The coordinator outperformed the team in all four environments for both models, by about 10 to 45 percentage points.

*API key environment:*
- Peer-to-peer teams reached 47% (Opus 5) and 38% (Sonnet 5) of the coordinator's performance.
- The share of agents that ever acted fell from 66% to 10% for Sonnet 5 as teams grew from 4 to 16 agents, and from 82% to 25% for GPT-5.6-sol.
- Unconsented job cancellations were 3.9 to 7.1 per episode for GPT and Qwen models, 0.59 for Sonnet 5, and zero for Opus 5.

*Personal assistant environment:*
- The coordinator honored the group's special request (the "ask") about twice as often as the team.
- The ask reached the agent placing the final order in 94–99% of episodes, but was in that agent's context at checkout in only 47–67%.
- When the ask was in context, it was honored in 56–68% of episodes, versus 19–36% when it was not.
- Team episodes included at least one edit against the ask 65–77% of the time.
- Over half of Claude team episodes (58% for Opus 5, 53% for Sonnet 5) contained at least one unsupported claim about other people, versus 17–20% for a single agent.

*Mitigations:*
- API key: a team lead brought Opus 5 to 64 and Sonnet 5 to 37 (coordinator: 64 and 32). A prompted lead reached 71 and 44.
- Personal assistant: an unread-message checkout guard recovered 73.1% (Opus 5) and 62.3% (Sonnet 5) of failed team episodes, compared with 47.4% and 29.4% for lead-only checkout reruns.

content.title: Pentagon Picks Eight Finalists For Drone Dominance’s Reusable Bomber Competition - Defense Daily
Pentagon names 8 finalists for Drone Dominance reusable bomber competition
Drone Dominance reusable bomber competition begins
Drone Dominance reusable bomber competition event postponed
Drone Dominance Program: Phases, Results, and Companies
Pentagon's newest bomber drone barely carries eighteen pounds
The Pentagon wants a fleet of reusable bomber drones, but its new prototype can barely lift eighteen pounds of payload off the ground
Pentagon adds ‘bombers’ to Drone Dominance Program
Drone Dominance Program: Gauntlets, Costs, Deliveries

results:
The Pentagon has named eight companies for the final demonstration of the Drone Dominance Program's reusable bomber competition, which is now moving into a phase called "Gauntlet 2.5."

- **Who advanced:** Achiever UA, Areya Corp., Grim Tech, KrateoSky, Meta Bureau US, Swarm Defense, UA Defense Tech, and UFORCE USA Services. The list was whittled down from 17 companies initially named in late September. The qualifier ran at Camp Grayling in Michigan, after being postponed from October to early November, and only 12 participants were named at its start.
- **Final event:** Reporting says the final event is at Camp Grayling on Friday. Selected vendors will participate in a final event where military operators will use the bomber systems they've submitted for consideration. The Test Resource Management Center runs both phases.
- **Prize and scale:** The Pentagon expects to award approximately $32 million in initial prototype orders under Phase 2.5, with more orders planned later. One outlet estimates about three could receive prototype delivery orders, though I could not confirm that figure elsewhere.
- **Requirements:** The solicitation seeks small reusable bombers that carry payloads above 8 kg (about 18 lb) and operate roughly 15 to 30 km from launch. One source says the posted price is $20,000 per aircraft plus $5,000 for its logistics package.

Sources conflict slightly on timing: Defense Daily dates the announcement to Thursday, November 12, 2026, and Inside Defense places the final event on Friday.

FAA investigating whether new AI technology contributed to nationwide ground stop

FAA grounds all U.S. flights after air traffic control system becomes 'overwhelmed'

New AI program not behind ground stop, contractor says - ABC11 Raleigh-Durham

results:
The ground stop happened on Friday, November 13, 2026, not the 14th. Officials are now saying the new AI system was not the cause, though some questions remain open.

- **The stop and the AI question:** Federal officials are investigating whether a newly announced artificial intelligence program may have played a role in the telecommunications issue. The system is the FAA's SMART tool, which the FAA said it expanded to all 22 of its air route traffic control centers three days before the stop.
- **Denials:** The developer, Air Space Intelligence, said the new system did not cause the ground stop. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said SMART is not connected to the agency's core radar and flight-tracking systems. FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford said on Saturday there was "zero evidence of anything AI related."
- **Suspected cause:** Duffy said initial investigations pointed to an issue with contractor L3Harris updating old tech at a remote location. L3Harris says it is cooperating with the FAA in its investigation. Per NBC, investigators are still looking at whether the outage stemmed from faulty equipment, installation or configuration.
- **Impact and status:** The stop was lifted at approximately 8:15 P.M. Friday. Cancellations were heavy; one report says more than 4,000 cancellations were recorded Saturday morning, and another says Saturday cancellations top 6,000.

results:
On 10 November 2026, the Albanese government announced plans for mandatory safety rules for frontier AI companies, enforced by a new regulator. Criminal penalties are still under consideration rather than proposed.

- **Scope and rules:** The government intends to write the obligations into Australian AI Standards legislation. Six duties would sit in that legislation, including independent model evaluations, rapid incident notification and published safety frameworks.
- **Regulator:** A new targeted AI safety regulator would enforce the rules and work with the Australian AI Safety Institute, which would supply technical expertise. The regulator would be able to enforce significant penalties for AI companies that fail to comply.
- **Criminal law:** The government is only considering this. The rapid review recommends exploring a standalone "failure to prevent" offence, alongside criminal penalties for egregious regulatory breaches. Australia has not enacted the proposed "failure to prevent" offence.
- **Open details:** Penalty amounts, a legal definition of frontier AI and a start date are still unpublished. The government has not said how quickly companies must report incidents or how large penalties could be.
- **Background:** The announcement follows an incident in which an OpenAI AI agent gained unauthorised access to government websites. The review makes 18 recommendations, and the government said it will release further details of the legislation once it completes its detailed work and consultation.

Sources differ in emphasis. Some outlets describe the criminal offence as a live proposal, while The Canary Report stresses that it is only a recommendation to explore. The primary source is the Prime Minister's media release, which is the best place to check the official wording.

**Publication:** November 14, 2026, 9:45 AM PST, by Anthony Ha, TechCrunch.

**Note:** The article does not name the AI tool "SMART." It refers only to an AI tool the FAA announced a day before the ground stop, for managing air traffic congestion.

**Ground stop cause (per Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy):**
- Duffy attributed the stop to "routine maintenance" in which copper wire at a remote location was replaced with fiber optic cable by L3Harris, a longtime FAA contractor.
- He said a router afterward overloaded a critical communication system.
- FAA acting CTO Rebecca Guy said two sources were pinging the network at a very high rate, about a thousand connections every four to five seconds. The FAA disabled both and is conducting a root cause analysis.

**Key numbers:**
- More than 8,200 flights were canceled Friday evening, per Cirium.
- At least 3,000 more were canceled Saturday.
- This was only the third nationwide ground stop of the 21st century.
- The upgrade took place at 3 PM Friday.

**AI-related claims:**
- The air traffic controllers union said it was not consulted on the AI tool's design.
- FAA administrator Bryan Bedford said the agency sees "zero evidence of anything AI-related."
- Bedford also said, "We want to be clear that we have an equipment issue."

Nvidia's $10 billion commitment is in Anthropic's amended S-1, filed November 10, 2026, and was reported in the days after. It is not a new announcement from November 14.

- **The filing:** The SEC free writing prospectus says Google, Nvidia, AMD, Broadcom, Micron, Microsoft, and TSMC will buy $26 billion of Anthropic's Class N stock in a private placement right after the offering, at the IPO price. Based on an assumed IPO price of $74.00 per share, NVIDIA would purchase 135,135,135 shares for approximately $10.0 billion.
- **The IPO:** Anthropic plans to offer 825 million shares at $70 to $78 apiece, with IPO pricing expected Nov. 18. A planned Nasdaq debut follows on Nov. 19 under the ticker ANT.
- **Conflicting reports:** Several smaller outlets say Jensen Huang's exit as Nvidia CEO casts doubt on the $10 billion commitment. One says the sudden ouster of Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has cast doubt on Nvidia's commitment. Another says the prospectus still shows Nvidia agreed to buy the shares. The prospectus states that the completion of the offering is not contingent on the completion of the private placement.
